summary: Structurally this is the weakest layer I examined: 176 of 276 public-schema policies (113 of 144 tables) are written in shapes that Postgres cannot turn into an index path, proven by `SET enable_seqscan=off` still choosing a Seq Scan. The two anti-patterns are a `(group_id)::text = <text GUC>` cast (47 policies) that disables the group_id btree every one of those 42 tables already has, and an `is_super_admin() OR (group_id = …)` disjunction (130 policies) that is unindexable even in its "fixed", sub-select-wrapped form. Compounding this, the five RLS helper functions carry `SET search_path`, which blocks SQL-function inlining and makes each unwrapped per-row call ~25x more expensive than the inline expression it wraps — and Supabase's own advisor is blind to all of it, reporting 5 `auth_rls_initplan` issues where 176 policies are affected. The saving grace is that none of this is currently costing much: `app_tenant` accounts for 16,881 of 3.4M statements (0.5%) and 19.7s of 19.7M ms (0.1%) over the 120-day pg_stat_statements window, because 379 `withAdminDb(` call sites run on a BYPASSRLS role versus 236 `withDb(`/`withTransaction(` — so these are latent, not burning, and cheap to fix while the tables are still small.

findings.title: 47 RLS policies on 42 tables cast group_id to text, disabling every group_id index in the tenant-isolation path
findings.evidence: Live prod qualifier (pg_policies, 47 policies / 42 tables, e.g. email_logs.rls_email_logs_group): `((group_id)::text = ( SELECT current_setting('app.current_group_id'::text, true)))`. All 42 tables have a leading btree on group_id and group_id is `uuid` on all 42 (verified via pg_attribute/pg_index join). EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) as app_tenant on email_logs (47,042 rows), letting the policy be the only filter: `Seq Scan on email_logs ... Filter: ((group_id)::text = (InitPlan 1).col1)`, rows=44,424 scanned, top-N heapsort, **Buffers: shared hit=1795**, exec 37-52 ms typical. Same query with the correct predicate `group_id = (SELECT NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_group_id',true),''))::uuid`: `Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id`, rows=20, **Buffers: shared hit=9**, exec 0.202/0.211/0.214 ms across three runs. Falsification: with `SET enable_seqscan=off` the live policy STILL produces `Seq Scan on email_logs (cost=10000000000.01..)` — the planner accepts a 10-billion penalty rather than use the index, proving no index path exists at all.
findings.impact: 199x more buffer accesses (1,795 vs 9) and 44,424 rows examined instead of 20 for the same 20-row page, on the largest table in the schema. Timing ratio observed between 180x and 3,500x depending on instance load. Cost is linear in table size, so it degrades exactly as the product succeeds. Currently latent because the read paths on these tables run on the BYPASSRLS pool (see the withAdminDb finding), so the moment tenant reads move onto app_tenant this becomes a user-visible regression on 42 tables at once.
findings.recommendation: One migration of `ALTER POLICY … USING (group_id = (SELECT NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_group_id', true), ''))::uuid)` across all 47 policies — cast the GUC to uuid, never the column to text. Note migration 20260827000000_156_investment_expenses.sql already uses the correct direction (`group_id = (current_setting('app.current_group_id', true))::uuid`), so the right pattern exists in-tree; it just needs the sub-select wrapper and to be applied to the other 46.

findings.title: 130 policies use `is_super_admin() OR (group_id = …)`, which is unindexable even after the recommended sub-select wrapping
findings.evidence: pg_policies: 130 policies across 72 tables match `qual ~ 'is_super_admin' AND qual ~ ' OR '`. Three EXPLAINs as app_tenant on email_logs, all with `SET enable_seqscan=off`: (a) `WHERE is_super_admin() OR group_id = app_current_group_id()` -> `Seq Scan`, 1,798 buffers; (b) the wrapped form `WHERE (SELECT is_super_admin()) OR group_id = (SELECT app_current_group_id())` -> STILL `Seq Scan`, 1,816 buffers; (c) the equality half alone `WHERE group_id = app_current_group_id()` -> `Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id`, `Index Cond: (group_id = app_current_group_id())`. Combined with the ::text family this makes 176 of 276 policies across 113 of 144 tables structurally unindexable (single pg_policies aggregate).
findings.impact: Every table carrying this policy shape is a guaranteed full scan whenever RLS is the only group filter. Critically, this is the shape the codebase would migrate TO if someone applied the standard Supabase `(select …)` advice to the ::text policies — wrapping fixes per-row function cost but not the missing index path, so a well-intentioned fix would leave the scan in place. The super-admin escape hatch is what costs the index, and it is exercised only by /api/admin/organization/* routes (lib/auth/middleware.ts:243 passes `role: bo.platformRole` into a TenantContext), i.e. a tiny fraction of the traffic that pays for it.
findings.recommendation: Do not just wrap these. Restructure so the tenant predicate is a bare indexable equality and super-admin reach is granted some other way — the simplest being to rely on the fact that super-admin traffic already runs on the BYPASSRLS `postgres` pool, and drop the `is_super_admin() OR` branch from group-scoped policies entirely. If the branch must stay, express it as a ScalarArrayOp (`group_id = ANY ((SELECT …)::uuid[]))`), which Postgres can drive an index scan from, rather than a boolean OR.

findings.title: `SET search_path` on the five RLS helper functions blocks SQL inlining, making each unwrapped per-row call ~25x more expensive than the expression it wraps
findings.evidence: pg_proc: app_current_group_id, app_current_organization_id, app_current_role, app_current_user_id, is_super_admin are all `LANGUAGE sql STABLE` with `proconfig = {search_path=public}` — a SET clause makes a SQL function non-inlinable, and EXPLAIN confirms it (the call appears un-expanded as `Filter: … is_super_admin()`, never as the underlying current_setting expression). 100,000-evaluation benchmark as app_tenant, run twice: `WHERE (g%2=0) OR is_super_admin()` = 2,008.9 ms then 1,953.8 ms; `WHERE (g%2=0) OR app_current_role()='super_admin'` = 463.6 ms; `WHERE (g%2=0) OR (NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_role',true),'') = 'super_admin')` = 78.2 ms then 77.5 ms. Baseline generate_series scan is ~70 ms, so marginal per-call cost is ~19.4 us (is_super_admin, two nested non-inlinable calls), ~3.9 us (app_current_role), ~0.08 us (inline). Policy counts calling these unwrapped: is_super_admin 99, app_current_group_id 66, app_current_role 38, app_current_organization_id 26, app_current_user_id 12.
findings.impact: ~19 us of pure overhead per row evaluated, on 99 policies. At the current 47k-row email_logs scale that is ~0.9 s per full scan of pure function-call overhead. is_super_admin() is doubly penalised because it calls app_current_role(), so each evaluation is two non-inlinable invocations. Also visible as InitPlan buffer hits in real plans: a single `is_super_admin()` InitPlan node reports `Buffers: shared hit=21` where the inline expression reports zero.
findings.recommendation: Two independent fixes, both worth doing: (1) wrap every call site in `(SELECT fn())` so it becomes a once-per-statement InitPlan instead of a per-row call — this is the change the 130 OR-shape policies need anyway; (2) drop `SET search_path` from the five helpers so they inline (they are SECURITY INVOKER and reference no tables, so search_path pinning buys nothing here). Fix (2) is a CREATE OR REPLACE — re-apply the REVOKEs afterwards, per the known grant-reset trap.

findings.title: Supabase's performance advisor reports 5 auth_rls_initplan issues where 176 policies are actually affected — the linter cannot see the project's own helper functions
findings.evidence: get_advisors(performance) returns 377 lints: 330 unused_index, 35 multiple_permissive_policies, 6 unindexed_foreign_keys, 5 auth_rls_initplan, 1 table_bloat. The 5 auth_rls_initplan hits are mpesa_callbacks.rls_mpesa_callbacks_admin, sms_provider_balances.rls_sms_balances_admin, contact_submissions.rls_contact_subs, feature_flags.feature_flags_write, investment_expenses.investment_expenses_group_isolation — all five call bare `current_setting()`. Zero lints for the 99 policies calling bare `is_super_admin()`, 66 calling `app_current_group_id()`, 38 calling `app_current_role()`, because the linter pattern only recognises `auth.<fn>()` and literal `current_setting()`. Zero lints for the 47 `(group_id)::text` policies, because index-usability of a policy qual is not something it checks at all.
findings.impact: A green-ish advisor has been treated as evidence that RLS is healthy. Migration 20260806040000_120_fix_auth_rls_initplan.sql was written directly against this advisor output (its header cites 'DB_PERFORMANCE_ADVISOR_AUDIT_2026-08.md (F3)') and fixed exactly the 6 policies the linter could see, while leaving 176 structurally worse ones untouched — and preserved the ::text cast in its own rewrite.
findings.recommendation: Stop treating advisor output as the RLS performance backlog. Add a repo-side check (a SQL assertion in CI against the migration-built schema) that fails on any policy whose qual matches `(group_id)::text`, or contains an unwrapped call to one of the five helpers, or ORs a non-column predicate against the tenant equality.

findings.title: Migration 131 silently reverted migration 120's RLS performance fix on three policies three days after it shipped
findings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806040000_120_fix_auth_rls_initplan.sql:37,43,49 wrapped current_setting in a sub-select for rls_sms_balances_admin, rls_contact_subs and rls_mpesa_callbacks_admin, describing itself as 'purely a cost fix'. supabase/migrations/20260809050000_131_recover_chairperson_rename_on_missed_policies.sql:28-38 then does DROP POLICY + CREATE POLICY on those same three, re-introducing the unwrapped form, under a header asserting 'Zero behavior change against production'. Live prod today: `SELECT qual FROM pg_policies WHERE policyname IN (...)` returns `(current_setting('app.current_role'::text, true) = ANY (ARRAY['super_admin'::text, 'chairperson'::text]))` — unwrapped — for all three, and today's get_advisors(performance) still lists all three under auth_rls_initplan.
findings.impact: The only three policies anyone has ever deliberately optimised are back in their pre-optimisation state, and the advisor has been reporting it for ~4 weeks. Direct runtime cost is small (mpesa_callbacks is 81 rows, sms_provider_balances and contact_submissions are smaller), but the process failure is the finding: a DROP+CREATE reverted a prior ALTER, exactly the same class as the already-banked 'CREATE OR REPLACE drops grants' lesson.
findings.recommendation: Re-apply the sub-select wrapping to the three policies, and fold the rule into the CI check from the advisor-blind-spot finding so a DROP+CREATE cannot silently regress it a third time. When a migration recreates a policy, it must recreate the current live definition, not the original one from the table's creating migration.

findings.title: meeting_attendance and meeting_resolutions each carry two byte-identical permissive policies, so the same qual is evaluated twice per row on every SELECT
findings.evidence: pg_policies on meeting_attendance: `attendance_read` (cmd=SELECT) and `attendance_write` (cmd=ALL) both have qual `((group_id)::text = ( SELECT current_setting('app.current_group_id'::text, true)))` — character-for-character identical. Same for meeting_resolutions (`resolutions_read` / `resolutions_write`). A FOR ALL policy's USING already covers SELECT, so the _read policies are pure duplication. Three more tables stack redundantly: organization_subscriptions evaluates unwrapped `is_super_admin()` in both `organization_subscriptions_admin_write` and `organization_subscriptions_select` on every SELECT; feature_flags ORs `feature_flags_read` (qual `true`) with `feature_flags_write`'s current_setting check, so the check can never change the outcome; platform_notifications ORs a write policy whose super_admin condition the read policy already contains. These are the 35 multiple_permissive_policies advisor warnings (5 tables x 7 roles).
findings.impact: Doubles the per-row policy evaluation on the two meeting tables and adds a wholly wasted unwrapped is_super_admin() (~19 us/row) to every organization_subscriptions SELECT. On feature_flags this matters most in practice: it is the second-most-called app_tenant query (`SELECT enabled, rollout_pct, applies_to, conditions FROM feature_flags WHERE key = $1`, 134 calls, mean 1.78 ms) and the redundant policy contributes nothing to the result.
findings.recommendation: DROP the four redundant policies (attendance_read, resolutions_read, and narrow organization_subscriptions_admin_write / feature_flags_write to their write commands with `FOR INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` instead of `FOR ALL`). Zero semantic change — verify by confirming the surviving qual is identical or strictly wider.

findings.title: RLS quals built on opaque STABLE functions destroy the planner's row estimates — 219 estimated vs 44,420 actual
findings.evidence: EXPLAIN as app_tenant on email_logs: `Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id (cost=0.68..3425.17 rows=219 width=16) (actual ... rows=44420 loops=1)` — a 203x underestimate. The same shape appears under the live policy: `Seq Scan (rows=224)` vs actual 44,416. The planner cannot see through `app_current_group_id()` / the GUC sub-select to the column's MCV list, so it falls back to default equality selectivity.
findings.impact: Harmless on a single-table scan, but this estimate feeds every join above it. At 47k rows the system is already 200x off; with a tenant-scoped join it will pick nested-loop plans sized for 219 rows and execute them 44,420 times. This is the mechanism behind the class of blow-up already seen in the fan-out bug — an estimate that is right in shape and catastrophically wrong in magnitude.
findings.recommendation: Falls out of the ::text and OR-shape fixes only partially — even the corrected `group_id = (SELECT …)::uuid` form is an opaque parameter to the planner. Mitigate by keeping the application's own explicit `WHERE group_id = $1` predicates (which DO get real selectivity from the MCV list) rather than relying on RLS to supply the filter, and by ensuring the tenant-scoped tables are analyzed — several of them have never been autovacuumed.

findings.title: The RLS layer guards 0.5% of database traffic: 379 withAdminDb (BYPASSRLS) call sites versus 236 withDb/withTransaction, including 43 tenant-facing /api/v1 routes
findings.evidence: `grep -rho 'withAdminDb(' lib app` = 379 occurrences across 112 files; `withDb(|withTransaction(` = 236 across 54 files. lib/db/index.ts:97,175 — withAdminDb uses the DATABASE_URL pool, and `SELECT rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles` confirms postgres=true, app_tenant=false. pg_stat_statements by role over its 120-day window (stats_reset 2026-05-07): postgres 3,048,472 calls / 12,995,410 ms; app_tenant 16,881 calls / 19,681 ms — 0.5% of calls, 0.1% of exec time. 43 route files under app/api/v1 import withAdminDb, including email/logs, sms/templates, mpesa/transactions. Concretely, app/api/v1/email/logs/route.ts:26-27 builds `conditions.push('group_id = $N')` by hand and runs it via withAdminDb at lines 41 and 53 — so `rls_email_logs_group`, the policy on the largest table in the schema, is never evaluated on its own read path.
findings.impact: The database maintains 278 policies, 80 never-scanned group_id indexes, and the per-row costs above for a mechanism that almost no production statement touches. Conversely it means every finding above is currently latent rather than active — which is the honest calibration for all of them, and also why now is the cheap moment to fix them. (The security reading of the same fact belongs to a different audit.)
findings.recommendation: Decide explicitly which layer owns tenant isolation. If RLS is the answer, the /api/v1 routes must move to withDb and the policies must be made indexable first (findings 1 and 2) or the migration will be a visible slowdown. If application-level `WHERE group_id = $1` is the answer, then the 176 unindexable policies are defence-in-depth whose cost should be minimised rather than optimised for — which still argues for the same rewrites, just at lower urgency.

findings.title: 80 group_id-leading indexes have never been scanned, including a 344 kB index on a 35k-row table whose RLS policy cannot use it
findings.evidence: `SELECT count(*), sum(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE schemaname='public' AND idx_scan=0 AND pg_get_indexdef(indexrelid) ~ 'btree \(group_id'` = 80 indexes, 1,256 kB. The starkest case: mpesa_reconciliations (35,430 rows, 7,120 kB) has `idx_reconciliations_group` (344 kB) with idx_scan=0, while pg_stat_user_tables shows the table taking 70 seq scans reading 276,970 tuples — and its RLS policy is `(group_id)::text = (SELECT current_setting(...))`, which cannot use that index. 38 of the 80 sit on the 42 tables carrying the ::text policy.
findings.impact: Write amplification with zero read benefit: every INSERT and non-HOT UPDATE on those 80 tables maintains an index nothing reads. Small in absolute terms today (1.3 MB), but it is a direct measure of the ::text policy's cost — the indexes were built for tenant isolation and tenant isolation is the one thing that cannot use them.
findings.recommendation: Do not drop these. Fix the policies (finding 1) and re-measure idx_scan after a week — most should start being used. Only then drop the ones still at zero. Dropping first would remove the very indexes the corrected policies need.

findings.title: withDb() spends three extra network round trips per tenant transaction setting GUCs one statement at a time
findings.evidence: lib/db/index.ts:125-130 issues `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE)` four times sequentially (user_id, group_id, role, and organization_id when present), inside a BEGIN/COMMIT opened at lines 143 and 146. pg_stat_statements confirms the ratio in production: app_tenant `SELECT set_config($1,$2,$3)` = 6,409 calls against `BEGIN` = 2,126 calls, i.e. 3.01 set_config statements per transaction. Server-side exec is trivial (mean 0.071 ms, 454 ms total), so the cost is entirely network: minimum 6 round trips through the Supavisor session pooler for a single tenant read.
findings.impact: Three avoidable round trips on every tenant request. Server-side cost is negligible; the user-visible cost is 3x the Vercel-to-Supabase RTT added to every request that touches the tenant pool, which I could not measure from here. Low severity today only because tenant traffic is ~560 calls/day.
findings.recommendation: Collapse into one statement: `SELECT set_config('app.current_user_id',$1,TRUE), set_config('app.current_group_id',$2,TRUE), set_config('app.current_role',$3,TRUE), set_config('app.current_organization_id',COALESCE($4,''),TRUE)`. Passing '' for a missing organization is already the sentinel app_current_organization_id() reads as absent, so the conditional branch at line 128 can go too.

findings.title: email_logs.provider_message_id has no index — this, not RLS, is what causes the table's 37.6M seq-scanned tuples
findings.evidence: `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE indexdef LIKE '%provider_message_id%') FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename='email_logs'` = 0. pg_stat_statements: `UPDATE email_logs SET status=$2, sent_at=COALESCE(sent_at, NOW()) WHERE provider_message_id=$1` — 1,063 calls, 19,316 ms total, mean 18.2 ms. pg_stat_user_tables: email_logs seq_scan=1,384, seq_tup_read=37,612,529 (avg 27,176 rows per scan) on a 47,030-row table. The 1,063 unindexed UPDATEs account for the large majority of those 1,384 scans.
findings.impact: ~19 s of cumulative exec time and 37.6M tuple reads. Reported here because I initially attributed email_logs' seq-scan volume to the ::text RLS policy and that attribution is wrong — this query runs via withAdminDb on the BYPASSRLS role, so RLS is not evaluated at all. Getting the attribution right matters for sizing the RLS findings honestly.
findings.recommendation: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_email_logs_provider_message_id ON email_logs (provider_message_id) WHERE provider_message_id IS NOT NULL;` Not an RLS fix — flagged so it is not double-counted against the RLS backlog.

findings.title: Five tables' RLS organization branch filters organization_id with no leading index on that column
findings.evidence: Cross-referencing pg_policies quals containing `organization_id = ` against pg_index leading columns: sms_usage_logs (394 rows), contributions (16), loans (4), groups (3) and loan_funding_splits all filter organization_id in a policy with no btree whose leading column is organization_id. Separately, get_advisors(performance) reports 6 unindexed foreign keys, none of them the RLS ones: investment_expenses.recorded_by, organization_subscriptions.assigned_by, sms_credit_ledger.created_by, sms_credit_ledger.payment_id, sms_credits.package_id, sms_opt_outs.actor_id.
findings.impact: Immaterial today — the largest of the five is 394 rows, so a seq scan is the correct plan regardless. It becomes real only if the organization axis grows, at which point it compounds with the OR-shape problem: contributions and loans use `group_id IN (SELECT group_id FROM organization_group_access WHERE organization_id = app_current_organization_id() …)`, a per-statement subquery on top of an already-unindexable OR.
findings.recommendation: Defer until the organization axis has data. When fixing the OR-shape policies (finding 2), add `CREATE INDEX … (organization_id)` on the five tables in the same migration rather than as separate work.
